pos: n. (John Spilsbery, c. 1593–c. 1668, Particular Baptist pastor of London)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through John; English Spilsbery, from a Midland place-name.
biblical_def: John Spilsbery was a cobbler who became one of the first Particular Baptist pastors in London, and in 1643 he published the earliest sustained English defence of the position this dictionary holds: that the proper subject of baptism is a professing believer, and that the ordinance signifies union with Christ in his death and resurrection. He signed the London Confession of 1644, which stated both the Reformed doctrines of grace and the baptism of believers only, and which went out of its way to profess loyalty to the civil magistrate because Munster was still what everybody meant by the word Anabaptist. The argument he made rests on the order Peter gave at Pentecost and never varied: repent, and be baptized (Act 2:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines baptize as to administer the sacrament of baptism, and profession as open declaration or avowal of one's belief.
webster_full: BAPTI'ZE, v.t. To administer the sacrament of baptism to; to christen.
PROFES'SION, n. Open declaration; public avowal or acknowledgment of one's sentiments or belief.
IMMER'SION, n. The act of putting into a fluid below the surface; the state of sinking into a fluid.
CONFES'SION, n. Acknowledgment; a declaration of one's belief; a formulary of articles of faith.
scriptures: Act 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
Act 8:37
And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Col 2:12
Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead.
corruption_summary: A cobbler who wrote the first English defence of believers' baptism, and signed the 1644 Confession.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the lumping of the English Particular Baptists with the Munster radicals under one word, which was done deliberately in the 1640s and is still done carelessly now. The 1644 Confession exists partly to refute it: seven congregations setting their names to the doctrines of grace, the lawfulness of the magistrate, and believers' baptism in the same document.

The principle to recover is the apostolic order, which places the profession before the washing. “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins” (Act 2:38). Philip states the condition and the eunuch meets it: “If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest” (Act 8:37). And the thing signified is a burial and a rising: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4).

pos: n. (Samuel Richardson, fl. 1643–1658, Particular Baptist writer of London)
etymology: Hebrew Shemuel, heard of God; English Richardson, son of Richard.
biblical_def: Samuel Richardson signed the London Confession of 1644 and spent the following fifteen years writing short, blunt pamphlets, most of them on two themes: that the Scriptures are sufficient without the additions of men, and that no magistrate has authority over a man's worship. His tract of fifty questions put to the Westminster divines on the magistrate's power in religion is the sharpest English statement of the Baptist position before Bunyan. He was a tradesman, not a scholar, and he wrote like one. The dictionary records him as part of the answer to the claim that liberty of conscience was a secular invention. It was argued first, in English, by men who held the doctrines of grace and reasoned from Scripture (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conscience as the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our actions, and persecution as the infliction of pain or death for adherence to a religious creed.
webster_full: CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
PERSECU'TION, n. The infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
SUFFI'CIENCY, n. The state of being adequate to the end proposed; qualification; competence.
PAM'PHLET, n. A small book consisting of a sheet of paper, or of a few sheets stitched together but not bound.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Fifty questions to the Westminster divines on the magistrate's power in religion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern account in which religious liberty arrives with the Enlightenment and is conceded to the churches by a secular state. The record is the other way round. Richardson, the English Baptists and Roger Williams argued it in the 1640s from the lordship of Christ over the conscience, and the argument they made is not the modern one: they did not say that truth is private, but that Christ alone is Lord of his church and the magistrate has no commission there.

The principle to recover is that the two spheres are distinct and the conscience is bound by Scripture alone. “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The question was put back to the authorities: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). And the division our Lord drew is the charter of the whole position: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).

pos: n. (Francis Cornwell, c. 1590–1665, Kentish minister and Baptist controversialist)
etymology: Latin Franciscus, a Frank, a free man; English Cornwell, from a place-name meaning corn spring.
biblical_def: Francis Cornwell was vicar of Marden in Kent, imprisoned for refusing the ceremonies, and while in prison he came to the conviction that infant baptism had no warrant in Scripture. He was rebaptized, left the parish church, and became the leading Baptist voice in Kent, publishing on the sufficiency of Scripture against the authority of tradition and persuading others, Christopher Blackwood among them, who had come to a public disputation intending to refute him. The dictionary notes the route by which he arrived. He did not start from a theory of the church; he started from a conviction about Scripture and followed it where it went, which is the way most of the English Baptists came to their position (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines warrant as authority, that which authorizes an act, and tradition as the delivery of opinions or practices from father to son.
webster_full: WAR'RANT, n. That which authorizes or justifies an act; authority; commission.
TRADI'TION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, by oral communication.
DISPUTA'TION, n. A reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something, or on opposite sides.
CONVIC'TION, n. The act of convincing, or compelling one to admit the truth of a charge or of a proposition.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Act 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: A Kentish vicar who read himself out of infant baptism in prison.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a change of practice must spring from a change of party. Cornwell had no Baptist congregation to join when the conviction came and no advantage in holding it; he was already in prison for a different nonconformity. He went to the texts, found no command or example of an infant baptized, and acted.

The principle to recover is that the practice of the church is tried by the written word, and that worship resting on tradition alone is vain however ancient. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Our Lord quotes Isaiah against exactly this: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). And the Bereans are commended for doing what Cornwell did: “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).

pos: n. (Christopher Blackwood, c. 1607–1670, Baptist pastor in Kent and Dublin)
etymology: Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; English Blackwood, from a place-name.
biblical_def: Christopher Blackwood went to a public disputation in Kent in 1644 to answer Francis Cornwell on infant baptism and came away persuaded against his own position. He was rebaptized, published The Storming of Antichrist within months, and spent the rest of his life as a Baptist pastor, first in Kent and then from 1653 in Dublin, where he served a congregation for seventeen years and wrote expositions of Matthew and of the Song of Solomon. The dictionary keeps him for the disputation. A minister who changes his practice because he has been shown the texts, at the cost of his living and his standing, is doing in public what the Bereans did in private, and it is rarer than it should be (Act 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines retract as to recall, to recant, and candor as openness of heart, frankness, freedom from prejudice.
webster_full: RETRACT', v.t. To recall, as a declaration, words or opinion; to recant; to take back.
CAN'DOR, n. Openness of heart; frankness; sincerity; freedom from prejudice or disguise.
DISPUTA'TION, n. A reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something, or on opposite sides.
EXPOSI'TION, n. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of a writing.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: He went to refute Cornwell and came away rebaptized, and went to Dublin for seventeen years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of a changed mind as a weakness of character, which makes public debate pointless and private study safer than either. Blackwood lost a parish living and gained a controversy. His later expositions show the same habit of mind at work on texts where nobody was watching.

The principle to recover is that proving is commanded and that the proving must be allowed to reach a verdict. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21). The Berean habit is set out as the pattern: “they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). And the standard is external to the disputant and to his party: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).

pos: n. (Daniel King, d. c. 1660, Particular Baptist evangelist of the Midlands)
etymology: Hebrew Daniel, God is my judge; English King, an occupational or nickname surname.
biblical_def: Daniel King was a Midlands Particular Baptist whose book A Way to Sion Sought Out and Found (1650) was published with a commendatory preface signed by William Kiffin, John Spilsbery and other London pastors, which is why it survives: it carried the weight of the London churches behind a provincial author. The book is a plain argument that a true church is a gathered company of visible saints, baptized on profession, walking under the discipline of Christ, and that such churches may be constituted where none exist. That last point was the practical question of the 1650s, when men convinced of these things found themselves in villages with no congregation to join. The pattern he appealed to is the one the Acts repeats (Act 2:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines constitute as to set up, to establish, to form or compose, and gathered as collected, assembled.
webster_full: CON'STITUTE, v.t. To set; to fix; to enact; to establish; to form or compose; to give formal existence to.
GATH'ERED, pp. Collected; assembled; drawn together.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. Instruction and government, comprehending the communication of knowledge and the regulation of practice.
COMMEND'ATORY, a. Which serves to commend; containing praise or recommendation.
scriptures: Act 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: A provincial author with the London pastors' names on his preface.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a church can be formed on affinity. King's argument has three marks and not one: a profession credibly made, baptism following it, and submission to discipline under Christ's rule. A company that has the first without the third is a meeting, and the seventeenth-century Baptists were as clear about that as any Presbyterian.

The principle to recover is that the gathered church has a visible membership and a real government. “Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls” (Act 2:41). Discipline has an appointed last court on earth: “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17). And the assembling is not optional: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).

pos: n. (John Tombes, 1603–1676, antipaedobaptist scholar of Bewdley)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through John; English Tombes, from Old French tombe, a tomb.
biblical_def: John Tombes was the most learned opponent of infant baptism England produced in that century, and the most awkward. Oxford-trained, a noted preacher at Magdalen Hall, he published in 1645 an examination of the argument for baptizing infants and spent thirty years defending it in print against Richard Baxter, Stephen Marshall, Richard Vines and others, always from the Greek, the Fathers and the history rather than from party. What makes him awkward is that he never left the parish ministry: he held his living, preached to a mixed congregation, and refused to administer infant baptism himself while declining to separate. The dictionary respects the learning, holds the conclusion, and does not follow the anomaly (Act 2:41).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines antipaedobaptist as one who denies the propriety of infant baptism, and anomaly as a deviation from the common rule.
webster_full: ANTIPAEDOBAP'TIST, n. One who is opposed to the baptism of infants.
ANOM'ALY, n. Irregularity; a deviation from the common rule; something abnormous.
EXAM'EN, n. Examination; a trial or close inquiry into the truth of a proposition.
LIV'ING, n. The benefice of a clergyman; estate appropriated to the support of a minister.
scriptures: Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
Act 8:37
And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: Thirty years against infant baptism in print, and he never left the parish church.
corruption_paragraphs: The anomaly is named rather than smoothed. Tombes argued that the baptism of infants has no command or example in Scripture, and then continued in a national church that practised it, on the ground that it was an error in administration and not a nullity of the church. The dictionary judges that the conclusion did not permit the compromise: a man persuaded that his congregation's members are unbaptized cannot consistently receive them to the Lord's table as baptized members, and the Particular Baptists who told him so had the better of the argument.

The principle to recover is the apostolic order, and the duty to follow a proved conclusion. “Then they that gladly received his word were baptized” (Act 2:41). The condition is a credible profession: “If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest” (Act 8:37). And the commission names the sequence: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them” (Mat 28:19), together with the charge to let a proof stand: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21).

pos: n. (Thomas Collier, fl. 1634–1691, Baptist evangelist of the West Country)
etymology: Aramaic Teoma, a twin, through Thomas; English Collier, a charcoal burner, a coal merchant.
biblical_def: Thomas Collier planted more Baptist churches than any other man in the west of England. From the 1640s he rode a circuit through Somerset, Devon, Dorset and Wiltshire preaching, baptizing and constituting congregations, and the Western Association of Baptist churches was largely his work. He also wrote a great deal, and in his later writings he departed from the orthodox doctrine of Christ's person, denying that the Son took his human nature from the substance of the virgin and holding views on the Trinity that his brethren judged unsound; Nehemiah Coxe answered him in print and the London churches disowned the teaching. The dictionary gives both. A man may plant churches by the dozen and still have to be answered by his own (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines itinerant as travelling, passing or travelling from place to place, and association as a confederacy or union of persons or churches.
webster_full: ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or travelling about a country; wandering; not settled; applied particularly to preachers.
ASSOCIA'TION, n. Union of persons in a company or society for some particular purpose; a confederacy of churches.
SUB'STANCE, n. Being; something existing by itself; that which underlies all outward manifestations.
UNSOUND', a. Not sound; defective; erroneous; not orthodox; as unsound doctrine.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Heb 2:14

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;
Heb 2:16
For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham.
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
corruption_summary: The west of England's great church planter, answered by his own brethren on Christ's humanity.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named because it is a grave one. To deny that the Son took his human nature from the substance of the virgin is to deny the ground on which he stands as our kinsman-redeemer, and the writer to the Hebrews argues the point at length and with deliberate emphasis on the word took. Collier's evangelistic labours were real and extensive, and that is precisely why his brethren had to answer him publicly rather than quietly: a man with a hundred congregations behind him teaches what he teaches to all of them.

The principle to recover is that the incarnation is a real assumption of our nature. “Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same” (Heb 2:14). The next argument narrows it to the seed of Abraham: “For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham” (Heb 2:16). And the standard that tries a church planter as surely as anyone: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).

pos: n. (Thomas Lambe, d. 1672, General Baptist pastor of Bell Alley, London)
etymology: Aramaic Teoma, a twin, through Thomas; English Lambe, a lamb, a shepherd's surname.
biblical_def: Thomas Lambe was a soap-boiler who pastored the General Baptist congregation in Bell Alley, Coleman Street, the noisiest and most open church in London in the 1640s. Anyone might speak; visitors came to argue; Leveller politics, universal redemption, free will and the laying on of hands were all debated on the premises, and a great many of the men who shaped English dissent passed through the room. He was imprisoned repeatedly. The dictionary records him as a General Baptist, which means Arminian, and that is a doctrinal error this dictionary names as error: the General Baptists held a universal atonement and a resistible grace, and Scripture says that no man can come except the Father draw him (Joh 6:44).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines general as relating to the whole kind or class, and free will as the power of directing our own actions without constraint.
webster_full: GEN'ERAL, a. Comprehending the whole species or kind; relating to the whole genus or class.
FREE WILL, n. The power of directing our own actions without constraint by necessity or fate.
AR'MINIANISM, n. The peculiar doctrines or tenets of the Arminians.
CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; usually, a meeting of dissenters from the established church, for religious worship.
scriptures: Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Eph 2:5
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
Joh 1:13
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
corruption_summary: The open church in Bell Alley, where anyone might speak and everyone did.
corruption_paragraphs: The Arminian error of the General Baptists is named plainly. They held that Christ died for all men without exception and that saving grace may be finally resisted, which makes the decisive difference in salvation the sinner's own, and the Scriptures deny it in terms that leave no room. The dictionary distinguishes this body from the Particular Baptists of the 1644 Confession, who held the doctrines of grace, and it does not pretend that the difference between them was a matter of emphasis.

The principle to recover is that the will of the creature is not the hinge of salvation. “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44). Paul states it as a conclusion: “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16). The dead are quickened, not assisted: “Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ” (Eph 2:5). And the new birth is traced to its source: “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13).

pos: n. (Henry Denne, c. 1606–1660, General Baptist preacher and army agitator)
etymology: Germanic Heimerich, ruler of the house, through Henry; English Denne, from Old English denn, a valley or swine pasture.
biblical_def: Henry Denne was a Cambridge graduate and parish curate who became a General Baptist preacher, was imprisoned for it, and then took the step that defines him: he joined the New Model Army and became an agitator for the Leveller party, was arrested after the Burford mutiny of 1649, and saved his own life by publishing a recantation and then preaching at the execution of the three men shot in his place. He returned to Baptist preaching and died in 1660. The dictionary records the whole course because it illustrates one thing exactly. A gospel ministry fused to a political programme serves the programme, and when the programme collapses the minister is left with the choice Denne made (Joh 18:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines agitator as one who agitates or stirs up, and sedition as a factious commotion of the people, a tumult.
webster_full: AG'ITATOR, n. One who agitates; one who stirs up or excites others; an insurgent.
SEDI'TION, n. A factious commotion of the people, a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law.
MU'TINY, n. An insurrection of soldiers or seamen against the authority of their commanders.
RECANTA'TION, n. A retraction; a declaration that contradicts a former one.
scriptures: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
corruption_summary: He preached at the execution of the men shot in his place.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named and it is not that Christians may take no interest in the justice of a government. It is the fusion of the ministry of the word with a political faction, so that the preaching becomes an instrument of the cause. The Levellers had real grievances and some real arguments, and Denne's pulpit became a platform; when the mutiny failed, the platform had nothing to stand on, and the pulpit went with it.

The principle to recover is that Christ's kingdom does not advance by the sword or by the faction. “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (Joh 18:36). The magistracy itself is God's ordinance and not the gospel's rival: “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). The sword recoils: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). And the snare that closed on him is named: “The fear of man bringeth a snare” (Pro 29:25).

usage: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) — a pulpit turned into a platform.
“all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) — Burford, 1649.
“The fear of man bringeth a snare” (Pro 29:25) — and a recantation that bought his life.

pos: n. (Thomas Grantham, 1634–1692, General Baptist messenger and apologist)
etymology: Aramaic Teoma, a twin, through Thomas; English Grantham, from the Lincolnshire town.
biblical_def: Thomas Grantham was the ablest of the later General Baptists: a Lincolnshire man of no university training who became a messenger of the churches, travelled constantly, suffered imprisonment, carried the General Baptist confession to Charles II in person in 1660, and in 1678 published Christianismus Primitivus, the fullest defence of his people's faith and order that they produced. He argued for believers' baptism, for liberty of conscience, and for a ministry supported by the churches, and he argued it with real knowledge of the Fathers and of history. He was also an Arminian, and the dictionary names that as error while recording the rest with respect. His case is the useful one: a brother to be answered, not an opponent to be dismissed (Rom 9:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines messenger as one who bears a message, and apology as a defence or vindication.
webster_full: MES'SENGER, n. One who bears a message or an errand; the bearer of a verbal or written communication.
APOL'OGY, n. A defense; something said or written in defense or extenuation of what appears to others wrong.
PRIM'ITIVE, a. Pertaining to the beginning or origin; original; first; ancient.
TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
scriptures: Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Act 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: He carried his people's confession to the king and wrote their best book, and he was Arminian.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named without erasing the man. Grantham held a universal atonement and a grace that may be finally resisted, which the Scriptures deny; and he also held believers' baptism, the authority of Scripture over tradition, liberty of conscience, and a disciplined church order, in all of which he was right and in some of which he was clearer than many Reformed writers of his day. Naming the one does not require suppressing the other, and a dictionary that could only praise men who agreed with it entirely would have very few entries.

The principle to recover is that mercy is sovereign and effectual. “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16). The drawing is not an invitation the sinner completes: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44). And where Grantham stood on the magistrate, he stood with the apostles: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
